name: Vestibular pathways and vestibulo-ocular reflex
modality: balance, spatial orientation and gaze stabilization
summary: Hair cells of the semicircular canals and otolith organs excite the vestibular ganglion neurons whose axons form the vestibular nerve to the four vestibular nuclei and directly to the flocculonodular lobe. The nuclei send excitatory and inhibitory projections through the MLF to the abducens, trochlear and oculomotor nuclei, producing the vestibulo-ocular reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation with a latency of a few milliseconds, descend as the vestibulospinal tracts for posture, and ascend through the thalamus to the vestibular cortex in the posterior insula and temporoparietal junction. Because the two labyrinths are balanced, a unilateral loss creates a bias interpreted as rotation (vertigo) with nystagmus beating away from the lesion.

origin.note: Hair cells of the three semicircular canal cristae and the utricular and saccular maculae; bipolar neurons of Scarpa's ganglion.

neuronChain.synapse: vestibular nuclei (superior, lateral, medial, inferior) and cerebellar flocculonodular lobe
ocular motor nuclei via the MLF; spinal cord via the vestibulospinal tracts; thalamus (VPL/VPI) for perception; cerebellum

decussation.level: MLF at the level of the vestibular nuclei
decussation.note: Each horizontal canal excites the contralateral abducens nucleus and, via its interneurons, the ipsilateral medial rectus.

waypoints.note: medial and superior nuclei for the VOR, lateral for posture
direct and indirect vestibulocerebellar fibers; VOR calibration
ascending to the ocular motor nuclei
vestibular cortex in the posterior insula (parieto-insular vestibular cortex) via the thalamus

termination: Extraocular motor nuclei (vestibulo-ocular reflex), spinal motor neurons (vestibulospinal reflexes), cerebellum, and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex for the perception of motion and verticality.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Acute vertigo, nausea, unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating away from the lesion, positive head impulse toward the lesion, falling toward the lesion
Oscillopsia with head movement and imbalance in the dark, no vertigo
Central vertigo with direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, skew deviation, normal head impulse, other medullary signs
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia with skew and vertical nystagmus
Gaze-evoked, downbeat or positional nystagmus, impaired pursuit and VOR cancellation
Tilt of the perceived vertical, lateropulsion, room-tilt illusion

pearls: HINTS beats early MRI for separating vestibular neuritis from stroke: normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew means central
Nystagmus from a peripheral lesion obeys Alexander's law and is suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus is not
The VOR is fast enough to keep your eyes on this text while you shake your head; a damaged VOR makes the world jump
